outgoing.name: 20th century
outgoing.excerpt: Despite a sort of golden age in the 20th century, snake charming is today in danger of dying out.

outgoing.name: Ancient Egypt
outgoing.excerpt: Ancient Egypt was home to one form of snake charming, though the practice as it exists today likely arose in India.

outgoing.name: Animal rights
outgoing.excerpt: Animal-rights groups have also made an impact by decrying what they deem to be the abuse of a number of endangered species.

outgoing.name: Market
outgoing.excerpt: Many snake charmers live a wandering existence, visiting towns and villages on market days and during festivals.

outgoing.name: Medicine
outgoing.excerpt: Charmers there mainly acted as magicians and healers.

outgoing.name: Middle East
outgoing.excerpt: It eventually spread throughout Southeast Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa.

outgoing.name: Mongoose
outgoing.excerpt: Sometimes, charmers stage mock combats between their snakes and other animals, such as mongooses.

outgoing.name: Tourism
outgoing.excerpt: Governments promoted the practice to draw tourism, and snake charmers were often sent overseas to perform at cultural festivals and for private patrons.
